chapter_theme: The eight heroic deeds of the Lord's might (பதிவலியில் வீரட்டம் எட்டு): the slaying of the asura, the punishing of Prajapati and Brahma, the overthrow of Jalandhara, the three cities, the elephant from the fire, Death at Kadavur and Kama at Korukkai. From the three cities on, Tirumular reads the deeds inwardly: the cities are the work of the three impurities, Death is burned in yoga, Kama destroyed by restraint.
structure_note: 339 to 342 tell four deeds as story; 343 turns, calling the literal reading foolish, and 344 to 346 give the remaining deeds with yogic or allegorical senses. The traditional eight sites (Kovalur, Pariyalur, Kandiyur, Virkudi, Athigai, Vazhuvur, Kadavur, Korukkai) are named only in 345 and 346.

339.reading: When the gods begged him, saying that an asura like Andhaka was tormenting all the lives of the world by the power of a boon, the Lord took the high-pointed trident in his hand and killed him.
339.nuance: Andhaka's slaying is traditionally set at Tirukkovalur. அந்தகன் தன்போல் அசுரன் can be 'an asura like Andhaka' or Andhaka himself; கருத்துறை, in the first line, is unclear.

340.reading: He struck off the head of Prajapati, who had erred in a matter of killing, and gave it to the fire; then, judging that the stable world needed him, he cut a head and joined it on.
340.nuance: Prajapati here is taken as Daksha, whose head was burned and replaced, in the legend, with a goat's. கொலையிற் பிழைத்த may mean 'who erred by killing', perhaps the animal of his sacrifice, or 'who escaped death'. The punishment ends in restoration.

341.reading: The gods who know the feet of the one who pervades everything and bears the great earth so that it stays: in that surging anger Brahma's head was severed, and there he took blood from Achyuta.
341.nuance: The legend, set at Kandiyur, is that Siva cut off Brahma's fifth head and filled the skull with Vishnu's blood. Whose anger surges (பொங்கும் சினம்) and how the gods in line 2 fit the sentence are unclear.

342.reading: The First, who mingles everywhere and rises in my heart, when Jalandhara swelled to make war on the reciter of the Vedas, drew a wheel there with his toe in the water.
342.nuance: In the legend, set at Virkudi, Siva drew a circle with his toe that became the discus which killed Jalandhara. நீர்மையின் is taken as 'in the water' or 'fittingly'. A variant reads யோகிபாற் (against the yogi) for யோதிபாற் (against the reciter).

343.reading: Fools say the Ancient One, with water in his red matted hair, burned the three cities; the three cities are the work of the three impurities, and who knows that it was these he shot?
343.nuance: The chapter's turning point: the myth is not denied but read as allegory, the cities being the soul's three bonds (traditionally anava, karma and maya). Tirumular calls the literal reading foolish, not the myth.

344.reading: At the sacrifice roaring with three fires lit, they did not know who Hara, wearer of the elephant's hide, was; and when the many gods who sought power were there, the killing arose from within that fire.
344.nuance: The legend, set at Vazhuvur, is that the sages of the Darukavana raised an elephant from their sacrificial fire to kill Siva, who flayed it and wore its hide. The verse names the elephant's hide and the killing from the fire; who the many gods are and who seeks power (சத்தி) is unclear.

345.reading: Turning the One who blazes at the root opening upward to the upper opening, with the breath joined, he burned Death in the yoga of fire: so Kadavur of the world became good.
345.nuance: The legend is of Siva kicking Death to save Markandeya at Tirukkadavur. Here it becomes yoga: the fire at the root opening (traditionally the muladhara) is raised by breath (கால்) to the upper opening, and Death is burned. The verse does not name kundalini; the reading is tradition's. கால் is also the leg, so காலுற்றுக் காலனை may pun on the kick.

346.reading: Making the mind that sat there settle in accord, turning back the way of the linga, destroying the work of Kama: that is the rare yoga of tapas seated at Korukkai.
346.nuance: The burning of Kama at Korukkai becomes restraint. இலிங்க வழியது போக்கி is traditionally taken as reversing the way of the sexual organ, holding the seed; it may also refer to the linga of worship. கொறுக்கை is Korukkai, with a likely pun on curbing.

links.note: 343 says the myth of the three cities is about the soul's impurities; 345 does the same for the slaying of Death, turning it into breath and fire raised in the body.
A third deed read inwardly: after the cities as impurities (343), the burning of Kama becomes the yogi's restraint of the mind and the linga's way.
Both tell Daksha's punishment by Siva: 340 the head cut and burned and restored, 353 the sacrifice broken by Siva's anger and the gods scattering.

source_issues: 342 line 3: பொங்குன்ய் is corrupt, probably for பொங்கும் or பொங்கு; variant யோகிபாற் for யோதிபாற் changes the victim of Jalandhara's attack from a Veda reciter to a yogi.
